title.en: Find the overall gain of a multistage amplifier
Compare RC, transformer and direct coupling
Choose a coupling method for a given use

say.en: A radio receives microvolts from its aerial but must drive a speaker. No single transistor gives that much gain, so we connect stages one after another. In this lesson: Find the overall gain of a multistage amplifier.
Compare RC, transformer and direct coupling.
Choose a coupling method for a given use.

body.en: When stages are cascaded, the output of one stage is the input of the next, so the *overall* voltage gain is the product $A = A_1 A_2 A_3 \dots$ (each gain taken with the loading of the next stage). In decibels the gains add: $G = G_1 + G_2 + G_3$. The bandwidth of a multistage amplifier is less than that of a single stage, because the gain of every stage falls at the band edges.

points.en: *Overall* bandwidth is less than one stage

narration.en: The overall gain of cascaded stages is the product of the stage gains, or the sum of their decibel gains.
narration.kn: ಬಹುಹಂತ ವರ್ಧಕದ ಒಟ್ಟು ವರ್ಧನೆ ಹಂತಗಳ ವರ್ಧನೆಗಳ ಗುಣಲಬ್ಧ; ಡೆಸಿಬೆಲ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಅವುಗಳ ಮೊತ್ತ. ಒಟ್ಟು ಬ್ಯಾಂಡ್‌ವಿಡ್ತ್ ಒಂದು ಹಂತಕ್ಕಿಂತ ಕಡಿಮೆ.

body.en: RC coupling uses a coupling capacitor and the collector resistor: it is cheap, compact and has a flat response over the audio range, so it is used in voltage amplifier stages; it cannot pass DC and gives poor impedance matching. Transformer coupling gives impedance matching and high efficiency (no DC loss in a collector resistor), so it suits power output stages; it is bulky, costly and has a poorer frequency response. *Direct coupling* joins stages without any capacitor or transformer, so it amplifies DC and very low frequencies; its operating point drifts with temperature. It is used in op-amps and DC amplifiers.

heading.en: Multistage Amplifiers, Frequency Response and Power Amplifiers

tagline.en: Cascading stages, the RC-coupled amplifier and its frequency response, bandwidth and half-power points, and the classes of power amplifier with their efficiencies.

myth.en: Class C is the most efficient, so it is the best choice for a music amplifier.

truth.en: Class C distorts the waveform badly; it is used only with a tuned LC load at radio frequencies. Audio uses class A, B or AB. High efficiency comes from conducting for only a small part of the cycle. The tank circuit restores a sine wave at one frequency, which works for an RF carrier but not for speech or music, which contain many frequencies.

say.en: Cascaded gain: A = A₁A₂…; in dB the stage gains add.
RC coupling for audio voltage amplifiers; transformer coupling for matching; direct coupling for DC.

Cut-off: gain = 0.707 A_mid (−3 dB, half power); BW = f₂ − f₁.
Max efficiency: class A 25% / 50%, class B 78.5%, class C above 90%.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. Three stages have voltage gains of 10, 20 and 30. Find the overall gain as a ratio and in dB.

say.en: Let us work this out together. Three stages have voltage gains of 10, 20 and 30. Find the overall gain as a ratio and in dB.
A equals 10 times 20 times 30 equals 6000.
Stage gains in dB: 20, 26.02, 29.54 dB.
Sum equals 75.56 dB, and 20 log 6000 equals 75.56 dB: they agree.
So the answer is 6000, about 75.6 dB.

narration.en: Let us work this out together. A two-stage amplifier has stage gains of 40 dB and 26 dB. Find the output for a 1 mV input.

say.en: Let us work this out together. A two-stage amplifier has stage gains of 40 dB and 26 dB. Find the output for a 1 mV input.
Total gain equals 40 plus 26 equals 66 dB.
As a ratio, A equals 10^(66 over 20) equals 1995.
vo equals 1995 times 1 mV is approximately 2.00 volts.
So the answer is About 2 volts.
